description: Questions extracted from this AI Atlas conversation; wording is labeled per case. Evidence references were checked in the preceding topic research, November 1, 2026. Candidate answers require human review.

cases.question: How does my local coding workflow compare with this browser/cloud workflow?
cases.originalExcerpt: im used to the workflow of vibe coding on local host with claude code them publishing it to github and making a pull request to merge, then publishing to github pages
cases.origin: Local/cloud topic request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: The development workbench moves from your computer to a remote workspace. Both can edit, test, preview, push a feature branch, review a pull request, merge, and deploy through GitHub Actions to Pages. A remote AI model can assist either workbench.
criteria: Shows where files, terminal, tests, and preview run in each workflow.
Shows the shared branch → PR → merge → Actions → Pages path.
Distinguishes assistant model location from workspace location.
cases.shortAnswer: Both workflows can use the same PR and deployment path. The main difference is where the files, terminal and preview run.

cases.question: Does cloud coding need setup again on every edit, making local iterations faster?
cases.originalExcerpt: right now you have to set everything up again but if its local vibe coding its much faster per iteration due to no need to setup cost
cases.origin: Local/cloud topic request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: A configured local project often reaches the first edit faster than a fresh cloud workspace. A warm cloud workspace can reuse tools and dependencies too. Startup, model waiting, build time, compute and network latency should be measured separately; one cold start does not establish every-edit performance.
criteria: Separates startup time from edit-to-preview time.
Explains reuse in a warm cloud workspace.
Avoids claiming local is always faster or cloud always rebuilds.
Acknowledges that new local environments also need setup.
cases.shortAnswer: A fresh workspace pays a startup cost. A warm cloud workspace can reuse its setup, just as a configured laptop does.

cases.question: What happens when the cloud workspace sleeps, and does the live website stop?
cases.originalExcerpt: everything on cloud (and earlier today the cloud was sleeping)
cases.origin: Local/cloud topic request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: Sleep or stopping may preserve files while processes need restarting; deletion or replacement can require reconstruction. The exact retention rules depend on the service. GitHub Pages serves the deployed website independently of the development workspace.
criteria: Separates sleep/resume from deletion/rebuild.
Does not assume Codespaces policies apply to Codex.
Explains why the published site can remain available while development sleeps.
cases.shortAnswer: A sleeping development workspace and the live website are separate. Published Pages files can stay available while development stops.

cases.question: What are the practical pros and cons of local and cloud coding?
cases.originalExcerpt: so i can see the differences and the pros and cons
cases.origin: Local/cloud topic request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: Local offers a familiar, reusable setup and no remote-terminal round trip, with hardware and maintenance constraints. Cloud can offer access from multiple devices, isolation, consistent images and remote compute, with startup, network, cost and retention trade-offs. Neither location by itself guarantees speed or reproducibility.
criteria: Compares startup, iteration, continuity, access, cost and data flow.
Includes drawbacks and useful scenarios for both.
Explains that hosted AI calls may transmit context even from a local workbench.
cases.shortAnswer: Local often wins on familiarity and startup. Cloud can help with access, isolation and compute; measure your actual workflow.

cases.question: What mental model helps me understand AI cloud deployment?
cases.originalExcerpt: if there's a better mental model to think through this help me format as well
cases.origin: Local/cloud topic request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: Start with workbench → repository → live site. Then ask three independent questions: where do I build, where does the app run, and where does inference run? A locally developed app can be cloud-hosted. An AI app using a secret API key generally needs a backend to protect it; static Pages hosting alone does not supply that backend.
criteria: Separates development, repository review, production hosting and inference.
Explains that local development can publish to cloud hosting.
Identifies that today’s Atlas is static and makes no runtime model calls.
cases.shortAnswer: Separate your workbench, source repository and live site. Model inference is another independent location choice.

cases.question: Can agents read shared repository instructions before starting work?
cases.originalExcerpt: create an md file in the repo because im using multiple agents to vibe code and they can read the instructions before they start work on the repo
cases.origin: Agent instructions and eval question-bank request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: The root AGENTS.md documents architecture, commands, source verification, collaboration, question-bank rules and the PR/deployment workflow. Compatible coding agents can discover it; other tools may need to be explicitly pointed to it. Reading a file is a convention, not an enforcement mechanism.
criteria: Root AGENTS.md exists and is linked from README.
Instructions describe actual commands and files.
Protects concurrent work and defines a handoff.
Does not claim every agent automatically reads or obeys it.
cases.shortAnswer: AGENTS.md records shared project policy. Ask each client what it loaded; discovery differs by tool and configuration.

cases.question: Can I review my questions and judge whether the answers are correct as an eval?
cases.originalExcerpt: a question bank of my questions in a separate page so i can verify if my questions were answered correctly as part of 'evals'
cases.origin: Agent instructions and eval question-bank request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: Each case preserves a user-question excerpt alongside a clearly labeled paraphrase, a proposed answer, acceptance criteria, evidence, and an answer link. You decide Pass or Needs work and record why. Reviews are saved in this browser and can be exported; they are not automatic factual verification or shared agent state.
criteria: Includes traceable user questions, not invented prompts.
Shows expected criteria and evidence separately from the candidate answer.
Defaults to Not reviewed and requires a human verdict.
Persists verdicts and notes, supports export, and flags older case revisions.
cases.shortAnswer: Review the proposed answer against evidence and criteria. Your verdict is a human review, not an automatic truth score.

cases.question: How do Claude Code and Codex work, where do they differ, and what happens from prompt to implementation?
cases.originalExcerpt: im interested in how claude code and codex works, and where it differs or whether its similar? what are the key steps it makes from prompt to implementation.
cases.origin: Coding-agent comparison request in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: Both combine a model, a harness, tools and a workspace in a feedback loop. A useful walkthrough is task framing, context inspection, action selection, tool execution, verification/revision and reviewable handoff. Their model families, interfaces, instruction loading and execution settings differ. Local vs cloud is a separate choice; deployment is a workflow step, not automatic proof of implementation quality.
criteria: Explains model vs harness vs tools vs workspace.
Shows a repeatable prompt → tool → observation loop, not just one-shot code generation.
Covers context, implementation, verification and handoff.
Describes sourced differences without a universal winner or local/cloud stereotype.
Distinguishes public architecture and illustrative examples from private model reasoning.
cases.shortAnswer: Both use a model → tool → observation loop. Compare the model, harness, context, permissions and result—not only the brand.

cases.question: Is GPT-6.1 Sol with a light setting right for all the tasks so far?
cases.originalExcerpt: also let me know if gpt 6.1 sol light is the right model for all the tasks so far
cases.origin: Model suitability question in this conversation
cases.proposedAnswer: It is a reasonable default hypothesis for routine edits, styling, documentation and straightforward tests. A higher reasoning setting may help with difficult debugging, architecture or source reconciliation. This is task-based guidance, not a measured comparison, and the active UI setting cannot be confirmed here. Compare real outputs and checks before deciding that one setting fits everything.
criteria: Does not claim to know an unobserved active model or UI setting.
Separates model choice from reasoning effort where supported.
Differentiates routine edits from harder tasks.
Treats recommendations as hypotheses without benchmark evidence.
cases.shortAnswer: A light setting is a reasonable routine-work default, not proof of suitability for every task. Test harder work at higher effort.

Uses the reported $20 price as a Plus assumption and still requests usage, reset time and expected workload.
Separates subscription limits, API spend and workspace compute.
Does not invent remaining allowance, prices or a within-budget guarantee.

cases.question: What happens inside a language model when I send a prompt?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: A common decoder language model turns token context into a distribution for the next token, repeatedly. Pretraining adjusts weights using many examples. Inference uses the learned weights to process the current context; an ordinary chat does not itself retrain the weights. Attention lets positions combine information from available context. Architectures differ, and reasoning/tool-use systems add surrounding steps. Fluent generation can still be unsupported by evidence.
criteria: Distinguish training from inference.
Explain tokens and context without calling them exact words.
Explain why plausibility is not factual verification.

cases.question: Why do tokens, context and output length affect product cost?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: Count every call, its input and billed output, then measure the cost per successful outcome. Token boundaries depend on the model’s tokenizer. Repeated history and tool outputs can be billed as later input. A context limit is capacity, not a budget or correctness guarantee. Subscription allowances, API billing and hosting costs are separate concepts. Reasoning accounting and cache pricing vary by provider.
criteria: Show units and all model calls.
Separate model cost from total cost.
Use logs rather than a word-count rule for real bills.

cases.question: Should I improve the prompt, add retrieval, or fine-tune?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: Diagnose the gap before changing the model. Product improvement and weight training are different levers. Prompting changes the instructions and examples supplied at inference. Retrieval supplies relevant external information; it does not update model weights. Fine-tuning adjusts weights with training data to shape behavior on a task. None guarantees correctness. Training needs supported tooling, rights to data, good examples, and a comparison against a simpler baseline.
criteria: Separate missing knowledge, inconsistent behavior and broken tooling.
Keep a held-out test set.
Measure new regressions as well as average improvement.

cases.question: How do I know whether retrieval is helping or hurting?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: Evaluate evidence retrieval separately from whether the final answer uses that evidence correctly. Semantic search can find related passages without matching exact keywords. Relevance alone does not prove freshness, authority, completeness or user permission. Chunking and ranking shape what reaches generation. A citation can exist without supporting the claim; inspect the passage, not just the link.
criteria: Test retrieval and grounded answering separately.
Include stale and unanswerable cases.
Apply permissions before exposing passages.

cases.question: How do I decide that an AI feature is good enough to ship?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: Define success for a user job, test representative segments, and set a release rule before reading the scores. Offline evals help compare versions; live outcomes test whether people benefit. Keep training examples separate from held-out evaluation. Use deterministic checks where possible and calibrate model judges against humans. A benchmark can help shortlist models but cannot replace your task set. Watch false positives, abstentions and costly rare failures.
criteria: Use observable criteria and representative cases.
Calibrate grading with human examples.
Separate offline scores from user outcomes.

cases.question: What belongs in an agent harness rather than the model?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: The model proposes actions; the surrounding system manages context, tools, permissions and the work loop. A fixed workflow follows predefined steps; a more autonomous agent chooses more of the sequence. More autonomy adds failure paths. Tool schemas, state, stopping conditions, retries and traces affect reliability. Give consequential writes a clear authorization path. A retry must not accidentally duplicate a payment or message.
criteria: Distinguish model and orchestration responsibilities.
Define stop and escalation conditions.
Handle retries without duplicating side effects.

evidence.label: OpenAI: unrolling the Codex agent loop

cases.question: How do I reduce cost and latency without quietly lowering quality?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: Compare cost per successful task and end-to-end latency, not just the cheapest token rate. Shorter outputs and fewer sequential calls can reduce waiting. Caching needs eligible reusable content and real hits; include write/storage fees when applicable. Routing and smaller models can save spend but need escalation quality checks. Batch work when delay is acceptable. Distillation and quantization are advanced options with quality and operational trade-offs, not automatic wins.
criteria: Use full workload cost and a stable quality threshold.
Distinguish perceived, first-token and total latency.
Include cache misses and retries.

cases.question: Where does value accumulate in the AI industry?
cases.wording: AI-generated follow-up; not a question attributed to you
cases.origin: Proactively generated from your PM-to-AI-PM learning goals
cases.proposedAnswer: Map compute, model access, data/tool infrastructure and applications; then ask who owns a valuable workflow. One company can span several layers. API access, open weights, distribution, proprietary data and integration depth create different trade-offs. Open weights do not imply zero operating cost or unrestricted licensing. Public market capitalization and private funding valuation are different measures; neither alone predicts product quality.
criteria: Separate facts from moat hypotheses.
Distinguish buyer, user and administrator.
Avoid rankings from incomparable valuations.

cases.question: Can this site use a database so I can mark questions done or archive them?
cases.originalExcerpt: can the preview site have a database? i want to be able to mark some of the questions as done so it dont have to appear permanently there or it can be archived
cases.origin: Question archive/database request in this conversation
cases.shortAnswer: Yes—a shared database needs a separate backend. Done/archive now uses browser-local storage, with restore and undo; it does not sync between devices.
cases.proposedAnswer: GitHub Pages serves static files, but its browser app can connect to an authenticated backend/database. You chose browser-local storage with no sign-in for now. The Done/Archive flow uses that storage: it removes questions from active views without deleting the public answer, preserves notes and verdicts, and offers restore, undo and export. A shared database and sign-in have not been provisioned. Cross-device private sync would require choosing and configuring a backend with per-user access controls; database secrets must never be embedded in the static website.
criteria: Distinguishes static hosting from a separate database/backend.
States that the current implementation is browser-local, not a shared database.
Explains done/archive, restore, undo and preservation of answer history.
Separates completion from correctness and keeps private data out of public repo writes.

cases.question: How is AI Atlas built: frontend, backend, hosting and languages?
cases.originalExcerpt: give me a simple systems design breakdown of this site so i can learn more about its architecture frontend and backend and hosting including the choice of coding langage used to built. add this to the question bank
cases.origin: Systems-design learning request in this conversation
cases.shortAnswer: HTML and CSS present the site; JavaScript runs the interactions. GitHub Pages serves static files. Node.js powers development/build checks, not a live backend. Personal state stays in browser storage.
cases.proposedAnswer: AI Atlas is a static frontend built with HTML, CSS and browser JavaScript modules, with public content in JSON. GitHub Actions runs Node.js tests and build scripts, then publishes the dist/ files to GitHub Pages. The browser fetches those files and saves personal notes, verdicts and Done/archive state in localStorage. There is no production application server, shared database, sign-in or runtime model API. The cloud coding workspace and Node preview server are development tools, separate from the published site. A future authenticated backend/database could add cross-device sync, but it has not been provisioned.
criteria: Shows the request and deployment flows separately.
Names HTML, CSS, JavaScript and the role of JSON, YAML and Markdown accurately.
Distinguishes Node.js development/build tooling from a production backend.
Explains browser-local state and its persistence limits.
Labels a future shared database as hypothetical, not currently deployed.

cases.question: How could AI Atlas support mobile, desktop and an optional shared database?
cases.originalExcerpt: if i want to scale it into mobile and desktop comaptible with database option tell me about the architecture and give me diagrams
cases.origin: Future-architecture learning question; you explicitly requested explanation only, not an implementation
cases.shortAnswer: The current responsive website already works in mobile and desktop browsers. Installed apps and cross-device data sync are separate choices; a shared database would sit behind authentication and an authorised API.
cases.proposedAnswer: For browser compatibility, keep one responsive HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend. If installation or deeper device integration becomes valuable, consider a PWA, a desktop wrapper, or a native/cross-platform mobile client; none automatically creates shared storage. For cross-device data, clients could use a shared authenticated API and per-user database records while public content remains on a CDN. Backend logic could use JavaScript/TypeScript or another suitable language; the database could be managed PostgreSQL. These are architectural options for learning only. No installed app, service worker, sign-in, API backend or shared database has been built or provisioned.
criteria: Distinguishes existing responsive browser support from hypothetical installed apps.
Separates client choice from database/sync choice.
Shows authentication, authorisation and per-user data boundaries.
Explains local/offline state and sync conflicts rather than assuming automatic sync.
Labels every future component as hypothetical and does not imply actual implementation.

designNotes.title: When is a responsive website enough?
designNotes.text: When reading answers, browsing players and basic capture are the main jobs. It avoids app-store releases and keeps one web frontend. The existing site is already responsive; no new app is required to read it on a phone.

designNotes.title: When might installed clients help?
designNotes.text: A PWA can add an app-like install/offline experience where supported. A desktop wrapper such as Tauri can package web UI with desktop integration. React Native is one option for native mobile UI using JavaScript; it is not a drop-in way to reuse every HTML/CSS screen. Each path adds release and support work.

designNotes.title: What might the backend use?
designNotes.text: JavaScript/TypeScript could reuse the team’s language; Python might fit a separate data/ML service. A managed PostgreSQL database is one possible data layer. These are examples, not a stack chosen or installed for Atlas.

designNotes.title: What would the data model look like?
designNotes.text: Keep public question content separate from private user state. An illustrative state record is (user_id, question_id, lifecycle, updated_at, version). Notes and preferences may need their own records. Enforce ownership in API/database rules rather than trusting a hidden frontend control.

designNotes.title: How should a PM choose?
designNotes.text: Start from the desired capability: screen compatibility, installation, OS features, offline use or cross-device sync. Add the smallest architectural change that enables it. More users or more content alone do not justify every client type and a backend.
